title: Lil Sebastian

jokes.text: Tom pitches a game show where contestants flip a coin to determine who performs vs. receives open-heart surgery, calling it 'Open-Heart Surgery'
jokes.setup: Tom is confidently pitching business ideas as if brainstorming a normal startup concept
jokes.punchline: The 'idea' is a lethal game show where random chance determines who dies on stage, presented with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: Strong cold-open energy. The joke works because Tom's entrepreneurial confidence is so misplaced — the business idea is genuinely horrifying but delivered like a TED Talk. The title being literally the thing is a nice economical touch. Good character integration: this brand of delusional hustle is quintessential Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm going to pitch a game show idea. It's called 'The Surgical Wheel of Destiny.' Contestants spin a giant wheel, and whatever body part it lands on, we perform emergency surgery on them. Live. On television.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: That's insane.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, I'm not done. If they survive, they win a cash prize. If they don't survive, their family gets a very nice fruit basket.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio pitches turning a Gulfstream G-IV jet (with wheels removed) into an apartment building so 'people could live inside their own private jet'
jokes.setup: Tom says Jean-Ralphio's bank account is 'blowing up' and they need business ideas
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio's idea is to gut a luxury jet and convert it into apartments — selling the fantasy of jet living to people who are definitely not on a jet
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'take the wheels off' and 'get 'em off of there' is funny — it's the detail of someone who has thought about this zero seconds but speaks with total conviction. Very Jean-Ralphio in character. Slightly less sharp than the surgery gag because it's more conventional 'dumb rich person idea.'

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Converting it into static housing defeats the entire purpose of owning a jet

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio: 'I made my money the old-fashioned way. I got run over by a Lexus.'
jokes.setup: The phrase 'I made my money the old-fashioned way' sets up the expected completion: 'I earned it'
jokes.punchline: He got run over by a Lexus — a personal injury lawsuit — which is immediately confirmed by the talking head
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode and one of the best Jean-Ralphio lines in the series. The misdirection is textbook perfect — the setup phrase is so familiar it autopilots the audience toward 'I earned it,' making the subversion land with maximum force. 'A Lexus' instead of just 'a car' adds brand-name absurdity that deepens the joke. Brutally economical: nine words do everything. This is genuinely comparable to the 8.0 anchor in quality and arguably exceeds it in structure.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Getting hit by a car for lawsuit money is the opposite of traditional wealth-building.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Do you want to get run over? Because I know a guy. Super gentle. Minor scrapes and bruises, major dollars and cents.'
jokes.setup: Ben points out Jean-Ralphio barely got hurt, expressing skepticism at the lawsuit windfall
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately offers to connect Ben with a professional 'gentle' hit-and-run operator as if this is a normal business referral
jokes.explanation: The callback to joke 3 escalates it beautifully — Tom has apparently already identified a professional insurance fraud driver, and presents it with the casualness of a Yelp recommendation. 'Super gentle' is a great detail. The rhyme of 'minor scrapes and bruises, major dollars and cents' gives it a sales-pitch rhythm that's very Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Yeah, so I'm expanding my business. I now offer insurance fraud consulting services.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: I got testimonials and everything. Here, listen to this one: 'Jean-Ralphio helped me fake my own death. Now I'm living in Costa Rica and my wife thinks I'm dead.' Five stars.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: And this one: 'I claimed my car was stolen seventeen times. It's the same car. Jean-Ralphio's a genius.' That's from my mom, but she's very credible.

jokes.text: Tom and Jean-Ralphio count down to say their shared thought simultaneously — Jean-Ralphio says 'spectacles' while Tom says '...spectacles' a beat late
jokes.setup: They build up to revealing their shared genius insight simultaneously
jokes.punchline: Tom is slightly out of sync, undermining the dramatic moment; both say 'spectacles' which is itself a grandiose but vague word
jokes.explanation: A gentle character beat showing how in-sync these two delusional dreamers are — they really do think alike. The slight timing gap (ellipsis before Tom's 'spectacles') is a subtle physical comedy note. Functional but not a standout.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I have a very special talent that very few people possess.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? What is it?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I can identify any type of leather by smell alone.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: That's stupid. I can eat an entire wheel of cheese in one sitting.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio names his company 'Entertainment 7Twenty' because 'you're willing to go around the world twice for your clients' — 2 × 360 = 720
jokes.setup: Tom asks why it's called 'Entertainment 7Twenty'
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio has done the math of 2 × 360 = 720 degrees to mean 'going around the world twice' — an entirely made-up metric for dedication that sounds vaguely numerical but means nothing
jokes.explanation: The joke rewards thinking about it — 720 degrees means you've gone in a complete circle twice, which means you're back where you started, which is an accidentally perfect metaphor for Jean-Ralphio's business model. The sincerity with which Tom responds 'That is unbelievable!' makes it land harder. Rewatch bonus because the math joke deepens on reflection.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What does 'Rent-a-Swag' even mean?

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: It's simple math, bro. 720 degrees is like going around the world twice, so you rent the swag, you go around the world twice, boom – Rent-a-Swag.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's not how degrees work.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Doesn't matter. The name is sick.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio tells Tom he needs him on his team and 'can't do this without you' — then immediately says 'Okay, I'll do it without you' when Tom hesitates for two seconds
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio delivers an impassioned 'I need you' speech about their partnership
jokes.punchline: Tom barely starts to express doubt before Jean-Ralphio instantly abandons the whole premise
jokes.explanation: The speed of the abandonment is the joke — Jean-Ralphio's emotional manipulation is so transparent and so short-lived that it exposes the hollowness of the whole 'I need you' bit. Perfect economy. The flat 'Okay, I'll do it without you' beats any elaborate comeback.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Li'l Sebastian, you were the best mini-horse in the whole world!

dialogue.speaker: Everyone
dialogue.line: Yeah!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We're going to miss you so much!

dialogue.speaker: Everyone
dialogue.line: We love you, Li'l Sebastian!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: This is the saddest thing that's ever happened to me.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: He was a real horse. A real American hero.

jokes.text: Leslie announces Li'l Sebastian's death and adds that in heaven he's doing 'the two things he loves doing the most: eating carrots and urinating freely'
jokes.setup: Leslie frames Sebastian's death with emotional sincerity and the comforting idea that he's now in heaven
jokes.punchline: His two heavenly activities are eating carrots and... urinating freely — the second item being absurdly specific and undignified for a memorial announcement
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional Leslie Knope characterization — her genuine earnestness about the horse's afterlife collides with total lack of filter about equine bodily functions. 'Urinating freely' is the perfect word choice: 'freely' implies the horse had urination restrictions in life, which opens a whole absurd implied story. The joke works on multiple levels and is completely specific to Leslie's character. High impact because the audience is in a tender moment before the rug pull.

jokes.text: Ron talking-head: 'When I walked in this morning and saw the flag was at half-mast, I thought: All right. Another bureaucrat ate it. But then I found out it was Li'l Sebastian. Half-mast is too high. Show some damned respect.'
jokes.setup: Ron explains his reaction to seeing the flag at half-mast
jokes.punchline: Ron's contempt for bureaucrats vs. his reverence for the horse — half-mast isn't respectful ENOUGH for the horse
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode and arguably one of the best Ron Swanson lines in the series. The structure is flawless: the setup establishes Ron's expected bureaucrat-contempt (funny but familiar), then the pivot — the horse deserves MORE mourning — lands as a surprise that's completely earned by Ron's established values. 'Half-mast is too high. Show some damned respect.' are two perfectly sequenced sentences. The joke is entirely impossible without Ron Swanson's specific character. Comparable in quality to the calibration anchors.

jokes.text: Ron's talking-head on death and self-reflection: ends with 'For Li'l Sebastian, I imagine it was good fresh oats, a trough of water, and a willing sexual partner. Or non-willing. He was a horse, so I think they had to do it either way.'
jokes.setup: Ron philosophically reflects on what we 'truly care about' when faced with mortality, building toward something dignified
jokes.punchline: The dignified reflection pivots to Ron matter-of-factly addressing horse sexual coercion with clinical detachment
jokes.explanation: Ron's deadpan willingness to go to a very dark and specific place — horse breeding coercion — during what's meant to be a sentimental reflection is peak character comedy. The 'or non-willing' clause lands as a jarring but logical observation from Ron's empirical worldview. Slightly less tight than joke 9 because it lingers a bit, but the darkness of the subject matter and Ron's total comfort with it makes it memorable.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie wanted me to tell you that you need to serenade her with a ukulele while doing the worm across the floor.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm not doing that.

jokes.text: Chris tells Ann that Leslie wanted him to 'kiss you deeply, which I'm going to have to pass on'
jokes.setup: Chris is delivering a message from Leslie to Ann; the note is a formality
jokes.punchline: Leslie apparently also asked Chris to kiss Ann deeply as part of the message relay, which Chris declines with professional regret
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Leslie would absolutely put 'also kiss them deeply' in a message delegation — it's completely in character — and Chris's polite professional decline is funny in its own right. The absurdity of the request and the straight-faced refusal creates a nice comedic gap.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, there are 47 post-it notes here. Each one has a different reason why you love me. And they're color-coded by category.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know. I ran out of wall space in my office, so I started on the bathroom mirror. Ben, you complete me. You're my soulmate, my best friend, my everything.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I love you too, but maybe we could express our love in a way that doesn't require industrial-strength adhesive remover?

jokes.text: Chris's talking-head reveals that Ben and Leslie 'secretly meet' in his office '...forty times a day'
jokes.setup: Chris casually mentions he likes his new part-time office and that his office-mate moved down the hall
jokes.punchline: He describes Ben and Leslie's secret rendezvous with a conspicuous pause and then the exaggerated count of 'forty times a day,' delivered with breezy acceptance
jokes.explanation: The ellipsis before 'forty times a day' is where the visual comedy lives — Chris's knowing pause. The exaggeration ('forty') is effective and his cheerful acceptance of being used as a love nest is characteristically Chris. Solid but not extraordinary.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: We're just holding hands and talking about our feelings. There's nothing wrong with that.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh my God, stop it. You're being so cute and supportive. That's disgusting. Just do something horrible to each other instead.

jokes.text: Ann sees the kiss monster Leslie drew on Ben's note and simply says 'Yeah.'
jokes.setup: Ben shows Ann the note Leslie gave him, which has a 'kiss monster' drawn on it
jokes.punchline: Ann's flat 'Yeah' is the perfect weary-but-fond reaction to Leslie's unhinged romantic enthusiasm, implying this is completely on-brand behavior
jokes.explanation: A quiet character beat. Ann's single 'Yeah' communicates years of friendship with Leslie in one syllable. Economy is perfect — anything more would ruin it. Visual gag bonus: we can infer the kiss monster drawing is magnificently unhinged from Leslie's standards.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm envisioning a sprawling memorial park with multiple tiers, fountains, maybe even a small amphitheater for community gatherings.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That sounds amazing. What's the budget?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Twelve dollars and thirty-seven cents.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We can make it work! We'll just use that as a down payment.

jokes.text: Ann about Ben and Leslie's secret workplace romance: 'You guys are totally welcome to use my office, just don't do anything on my desk.' Ben: 'Oh, we don't... You know. We just like to work in the same place, and then we talk and hold hands.' Ann: 'Yuck, that's somehow worse.'
jokes.setup: Ann generously offers her office for the secret romance while setting a boundary about the desk
jokes.punchline: Ben's innocent description of their activities (talking and holding hands) is somehow more nauseating to Ann than whatever she imagined them doing
jokes.explanation: 'That's somehow worse' is an excellent punchline because it inverts the expected joke structure — we anticipate Ann being grossed out by physical intimacy, but sweet wholesome hand-holding is more nauseating to her as a single person. The follow-up 'Yeah, it sounded bad when I said it' from Ben adds a nice self-aware button. Good character work: Ann's cynicism and Ben's earnestness are both perfectly captured.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, did you get your memo about Li'l Sebastian?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yeah, I got it. Very thorough, very official.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Did you read all of it?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Of course. Wait... what is this? 'Ben, you are the Li'l Sebastian to my heart'?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Keep reading.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: 'Every day with you is a majestic pony ride through the fields of my soul.'

jokes.text: Leslie declares the memorial should 'rival the Super Bowl half-time show' — immediately followed by 'Also, the budget is $600.'
jokes.setup: Leslie passionately calls for a memorial that rivals the Super Bowl halftime show
jokes.punchline: Hard cut to the budget reveal: $600
jokes.explanation: Classic Parks and Rec structural joke: grand ambition meets government-budget reality. The economy here is perfect — no extra words between the aspiration and the deflation. 'Also' as the transition word does a lot of comedic work, making it sound like a minor footnote when it's actually a catastrophic constraint. Strong structural execution of a familiar premise.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That memo was about... municipal efficiency! Yes, a passionate plea for better filing systems.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, and Jerry, you know what? You're like a filing cabinet, but instead of organizing documents, you just organize confusion. And disappointment. You're a disappointment cabinet.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I... what?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: A walking, talking monument to incompetence. If inefficiency was an Olympic sport, you'd somehow still come in last place.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Hey, if you want a song from Andy Dwyer, lead singer of Mouse Rat, you should know he doesn't get out of bed for less than $1,000.' Leslie: 'Well, he sleeps on a futon, so we can give him 50 bucks.' Andy: 'Sold.'
jokes.setup: Andy grandiosely refers to himself in the third person and names an outrageous price floor for his artistic services
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately undercuts it with specific domestic knowledge (the futon) and pays 5% of his stated minimum; Andy instantly caves
jokes.explanation: Three-part structure executed perfectly. Andy's third-person grandiosity sets up a false sense of his leverage; Leslie's 'he sleeps on a futon' uses real-world knowledge to destroy the illusion in one move; Andy's immediate 'Sold' confirms he has no actual leverage and no self-awareness. The futon detail is both funny in itself and a callback to Andy's poverty, making this feel earned rather than cheap. One of the tighter comedic exchanges in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Cube butt! Cube butt!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Cube butt!

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Cube butt!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Cube butt!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Cube butt!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Cube butt!

dialogue.speaker: Everyone
dialogue.line: Cube butt! Cube butt! Cube butt!

jokes.text: Leslie's memo to Ben reads 'You have a cute butt.' Jerry's memo apparently lists facts about Li'l Sebastian but his also says 'You have a cute butt.' Ben says it's 'probably a typo' — probably meant 'cube butt' because Jerry's butt is shaped like a cube.
jokes.setup: Leslie distributed memos with Sebastian facts; Ben notices his says 'You have a cute butt'
jokes.punchline: It's revealed Jerry also received the same note, but Ben re-interprets it as a typo meaning 'cube butt' — inventing an insult about Jerry's butt being cube-shaped
jokes.explanation: Multi-layered joke: first layer is Leslie secretly flirting with Ben via government memo; second layer is the Jerry pivot where the same line becomes a brutal insult via 'typo' wordplay; third layer is 'cube butt' as a completely invented and geometrically specific insult. The 'cube butt' invention is particularly good — it sounds like something that could only make sense in this specific deflection.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: Well, the good news is you have tendonitis, not a severed tendon.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: That's good news?

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: I mean, I was just comparing it to something I made up.

jokes.text: Jerry repeats 'cube butt' to himself in a talking-head with confusion, while off-camera voices taunt 'Cube butt, cube butt'
jokes.setup: The 'cube butt' insult was established in the previous scene
jokes.punchline: Jerry is still processing it in his talking-head while unknown voices offscreen are already chanting it — the workplace has absorbed the insult instantly
jokes.explanation: The callback lands because the offscreen chanting shows how instantly the insult became communal — the office has already weaponized it before Jerry can even process it. Solid Jerry-abuse gag. The visual of Jerry's bewildered talking-head face while 'cube butt' echoes around him plays well.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Doctor, I've been experiencing occasional fatigue and I'm worried it might be something serious. Could it be my heart? My lungs? My pancreas?

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: Mr. Traeger, you're in perfect health. You're one of the healthiest patients I've ever seen.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Perfect health? That's impossible. Nobody's in perfect health. That means I'm about to have a catastrophic medical event. This is the worst day of my life.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: No, it's actually the best day of your life.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: How is that the best day of my life? I came here expecting answers!

jokes.text: Doctor tells Chris the good news is it's 'just tendonitis' — Chris asks 'How is that good news?' — Doctor: 'The other option was shoulder cancer.'
jokes.setup: The doctor tries to frame tendonitis as the 'good news'
jokes.punchline: The alternative diagnosis was shoulder cancer — making tendonitis good news by contrast
jokes.explanation: Good structure: the 'good news is' frame creates expectation of something genuinely reassuring; the alternative 'shoulder cancer' recontextualizes everything. The casual specificity of 'shoulder cancer' is funnier than just 'cancer' — it's oddly precise and sounds like something doctors don't actually say. Economy is strong.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You don't understand. Li'l Sebastian was more than just a horse. He was a symbol of Pawnee's spirit, our hopes and dreams.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, it was a pony.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A pony?! Ben, Li'l Sebastian changed lives.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm sure he was very... small. And horse-like.

jokes.text: Doctor: 'Little things like this happen with men of your age.' Chris: 'Men of my age? How old do you think I am?' Doctor: 'Forty-two.' Chris: 'I am 44, and I plan to live to be 150.'
jokes.setup: The doctor makes a comment about Chris's age triggering Chris's vanity
jokes.punchline: Chris corrects a two-year underestimate of his age while announcing he plans to live to 150 in the same breath
jokes.explanation: The joke has two prongs: Chris is offended the doctor guessed he's 42 when he's 44 (he wanted to be told younger, not older), and he responds to the existential challenge by announcing he'll live to 150. Both responses are absolutely Chris Traeger — the physical vanity and the superhuman positivity as a defense mechanism. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jean-Ralphio, you're like a strip club. Fun for a night, but ultimately empty and bad for you.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Hey!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. Strip clubs have a four-drink minimum and a two-drink maximum. They're very organized establishments with clear boundaries and excellent customer service.

jokes.text: Chris asks what the cure for tendonitis is; Doctor says: 'Get a time machine. Go back to being 20.'
jokes.setup: Chris optimistically asks what the cure is
jokes.punchline: The doctor's prescription is to get a time machine — a sarcastically bleak non-answer that essentially says 'you're just old'
jokes.explanation: The deadpan nihilism of the time machine prescription is funny and characterizes the doctor as someone who has stopped trying to coddle patients. Perfect economy — two sentences, no setup wasted. The mean doctor character as a foil for Chris's toxic positivity is well-deployed here.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I just realized that horse died of colic, which is basically just stomach pain. I get stomach pain all the time. I'm basically a horse.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Well, we should probably run some tests then.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: What kind of tests?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I don't know, whatever they did for the horse. Maybe we need to put you down.

jokes.text: Chris: 'Dr. Harris, you are literally the meanest person I have ever met.'
jokes.setup: Dr. Harris has been brutally honest and mildly mean throughout the appointment
jokes.punchline: Chris — a man of infinite positivity who finds goodness in everyone — declares this doctor the literal meanest person he's ever encountered, which contextualizes the doctor's mundane meanness as cosmically significant
jokes.explanation: Works because of character context: if Chris Traeger says you're the meanest person he's ever met, that's actually a significant claim given his relentless optimism. The hyperbole lands because Chris is the opposite of hyperbolic about negative assessments. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Leslie, we need to talk about us. About what's been happening between us.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? There's nothing happening. Nothing at all. I don't know what you're talking about.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Leslie, come on. I know you feel it too.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Feel what? I don't feel anything! I've never felt anything! With anyone! Ever! I've never had sex with anyone in my entire life!

jokes.text: Ben says flatly: 'Okay, all the permits cleared for the horse funeral.' Then adds: 'What was that tone? What? Oh, nothing. I'm very sad about this.'
jokes.setup: Ben delivers bureaucratic news about permit clearance for a horse funeral
jokes.punchline: Someone (off-screen) notices his tone; Ben deflects but clearly isn't that sad about the horse, before correcting himself
jokes.explanation: A recurring gag in this episode: Ben is one of the few people who doesn't understand why Li'l Sebastian is so beloved, and his flat bureaucratic delivery betrays it. The self-correction 'I'm very sad about this' is a nice social-cover beat. Functional but slight.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I didn't do it! In fact, Chris, YOU did it!

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: What? No I didn't!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes you did, and I have witnesses. Checkmate.

jokes.text: Tom announces Jean-Ralphio will put on the memorial 'pro bono, just for the pub.' He then explains: 'Pub is an abbreviation for publicity.'
jokes.setup: Tom is excited about Jean-Ralphio's free offer.
jokes.punchline: Tom stops to explain that 'pub' is short for 'publicity' — treating the room like they wouldn't know this basic abbreviation.
jokes.explanation: Tom's condescension about basic vocabulary is in character, and the self-importance of explaining 'pub' is funny in its smallness. Classic Tom Haverford energy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I found out about you two when I overheard you in the office after hours.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh God, what did you hear?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You were having some kind of historical figure roleplay. You were Benjamin Franklin, Ben was Thomas Jefferson, and you were arguing about whether the Constitution should have a clause about waffles.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: In my defense, the Founding Fathers loved breakfast foods.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It was educational!

jokes.text: Ron: 'Jean-Ralphio is a clown. This is the memorial for Li'l Sebastian, not double-coupon night at a strip club.'
jokes.setup: Tom pitches letting Jean-Ralphio run the memorial for publicity
jokes.punchline: Ron's objection escalates from 'clown' to a bizarrely specific comparison: 'double-coupon night at a strip club'
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'double-coupon night at a strip club' is what elevates this well above a generic Ron insult. It implies Ron knows exactly what double-coupon night at a strip club is like — and how it contrasts with dignity. The line works on three levels: it insults Jean-Ralphio, it characterizes Ron (he has been to these places), and it sets the aesthetic stakes for what the memorial should NOT be. Very quotable. One of the episode's sharper one-liners.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Mr. Ambassador, I've been following your voting record on environmental protection...

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Well, I do care deeply about our planet's future.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Maybe we could discuss it over dinner? Somewhere private?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, is this a conflict of interest?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Only if you don't vote yes on my infrastructure bill.

jokes.text: Tom: 'First off, double-coupon night is an incredible value.'
jokes.setup: Ron dismisses Jean-Ralphio's involvement using the 'double-coupon night at a strip club' comparison
jokes.punchline: Tom defends the concept of double-coupon night at a strip club as sound economics before getting to his actual argument
jokes.explanation: Perfect comedic judo — Tom takes Ron's insult and instead of refuting it, validates the underlying premise (double-coupon night IS a good deal) before moving to his actual point. The pivot reveals Tom has been to many double-coupon nights. The economy is exceptional: one sentence reveals Tom's values, his relationship to strip clubs, and his argument style. One of the episode's best one-liners.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: A horse with no name walked into a bar. The bartender said, 'Why the long face?' The horse said, 'Because I have no name.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That doesn't make sense. Horses can't talk.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Exactly! That's why he needs to learn!

jokes.text: Leslie tells Tom 'Make us proud.' Then Ron says quietly to Tom 'Make him proud.' Camera reveals Leslie has already walked away — Ron is indicating a framed photo of Li'l Sebastian
jokes.setup: Leslie gives Tom an emotional send-off about making them proud
jokes.punchline: Ron redirects Tom's accountability to the framed photo of the horse, which is the more important party in Ron's worldview
jokes.explanation: The visual gag of Ron indicating the framed photo — and the implication that the HORSE holds Tom to a higher standard than Leslie does — is pure Ron Swanson. The joke requires no explanation; it works entirely through Ron's relationship with Li'l Sebastian. Strong character integration and a visual that's funnier in the watching than in description.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: We gather here today to celebrate a life well lived, so let me play you a little song I wrote.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Life is short and then you die, nothing matters in the end, we're all just worm food, my friends.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Dust to dust and bones to clay, we're all rotting every day, eventually we'll decompose and fade away.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So cherish the time that you have left before the darkness comes and takes your final breath.

jokes.text: Tom asks about removing something from a photo: 'Why don't you just Photoshop that out?' (implying someone photobombed or something is wrong with a memorial image)
jokes.setup: The group is looking at what appears to be a memorial photo of Li'l Sebastian
jokes.punchline: Tom's instinct for any problem is 'just Photoshop it' — a trivializing tech-solution response to a solemn situation
jokes.explanation: A minor gag. 'Just Photoshop that out' is a bit too generic — could be said by any modern character in any show. The character integration is minimal. Passes without much impression.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Jerry, you gotta pick one. We need a ribbon color for the memorial.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Well, I'm thinking we go with the Midnight Obsidian.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's just black, Jerry.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: No, no. Or maybe the Ebony Noir?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Also black.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: What about Charcoal Shadow?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Jerry, they're all just different blacks!

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio is shocked to hear Li'l Sebastian died, then speculates: 'Like tendonitis?' when Ann mentions the horse 'had a lot of ailments'
jokes.setup: Ann mentions Sebastian had ailments in old age
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio, who is currently hypochondriacally worried about his own tendonitis, asks if the horse maybe also had tendonitis — collapsing the distance between himself and a deceased miniature horse
jokes.explanation: This callback works cross-character: Jean-Ralphio is connecting Chris's diagnosis to the dead horse. The absurdity of equating himself medically with Li'l Sebastian is very Jean-Ralphio. Also plants the tendonitis thread that pays off later with Chris and Ann.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Ann, I need to ask you something really important.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh my god, what is it?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Do you think my heart rate is elevated? I've been feeling a flutter in my chest all morning.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Chris, you're fine.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: But what if it's arrhythmia? Or early-onset cardiomyopathy?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: It's just more of his health anxiety, not anything relationship-related.

jokes.text: Ann: 'I don't have his chart in front of me.' Jean-Ralphio: 'Could you get it?' Ann: 'What? No... There's no chart.' Jean-Ralphio: 'Oh, my God. Death is inescapable. Goodbye, Ann Perkins.'
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio asks Ann to retrieve Li'l Sebastian's medical chart
jokes.punchline: Ann patiently explains there is no chart; Jean-Ralphio interprets the missing chart as existential evidence that death comes for us all, then dramatically exits
jokes.explanation: Jean-Ralphio's leap from 'there's no chart' to 'death is inescapable' is a beautifully absurd piece of logic. It escalates from mundane confusion to existential crisis in under three sentences. 'Goodbye, Ann Perkins' — using her full name — is the perfect melodramatic button. This is peak Jean-Ralphio: maximum drama from minimal stimulus.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? No, we were just... Ben was helping me with my... my Fulbright application!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yes, that's right. Leslie won a Fulbright scholarship.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: One of the most prestigious intellectual awards in America.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: We should probably tell people about this.

jokes.text: Leslie tells Ann she feels her life is 'almost perfect' but they have to sneak around, then adds 'weirdly, it's kind of fun that nobody knows'
jokes.setup: Leslie says their secret romance is an inconvenience but kind of fun
jokes.punchline: The camera (and audience) knows that Chris already found out via butt-dial, making 'it's kind of fun that nobody knows' immediately ironic — this is a dramatic irony setup for the Chris reveal coming seconds later
jokes.explanation: The joke here is structural/dramatic irony — Leslie's statement is about to be immediately contradicted. On rewatch, the irony is delicious. On first watch, it works as mild dramatic setup. The rewatch value is high.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: We've gathered here today to celebrate the life of—

dialogue.speaker: Horse
dialogue.line: *defecates loudly during ceremony*

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Well, I think that's what he would have wanted.

jokes.text: Chris appears behind Leslie and asks 'How long have you been sleeping with Ben?' — Leslie panics and says 'I've never had sex with anyone anywhere... You have the nerve, the audacity... Ben is my boss, technically. And he is terrible, facewise.'
jokes.setup: Chris ambushes Leslie with the question about her relationship with Ben
jokes.punchline: Leslie's panic generates a cascade of self-contradicting denials including 'I've never had sex with anyone anywhere' and calling Ben 'terrible, facewise' — escalating into incoherent misdirection
jokes.explanation: Amy Poehler's panic spiral is a masterpiece of character-specific improvised-sounding escalation. 'I've never had sex with anyone anywhere' is absurdly sweeping. 'Ben is my boss, technically' is a weird legalistic hedge. 'He is terrible, facewise' is the best of them — a desperate attempt to cast doubt on the plausibility of the relationship by insulting Ben's appearance, which she doesn't believe at all. The escalation and the progressive incoherence are perfectly constructed. Very high character integration: this is exactly how Leslie Knope would panic.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'How do I know, frankly, that you're not sleeping with him? Maybe you are. Maybe you're trying to throw me off. Hmm. Check and mate.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is panicking and looking for any way to redirect suspicion away from herself
jokes.punchline: She accuses Chris of sleeping with Ben as a deflection, then declares victory with 'Check and mate' as if she's logically cornered him
jokes.explanation: The 'Check and mate' button on an entirely nonsensical accusation is perfect Leslie logic: she has no actual argument but she's declared herself the winner of it. This is Leslie at her most frantic and most herself — she turns absurd desperation into bureaucratic confidence. Highly quotable line.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: He doesn't even know what kind of animal Li'l Sebastian was

jokes.text: Chris reveals he found out about Ben and Leslie because 'Ben butt-dialed me last night.' Audio of their roleplay follows: 'Okay, and this is how Eleanor Roosevelt would kiss.' Chris: 'Whoa. Eleanor likes the tongue.'
jokes.setup: Chris says he found out via butt-dial
jokes.punchline: The butt-dial captured Ben and Leslie doing presidential roleplay — specifically Eleanor Roosevelt making out with enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's comedic peak for the Ben/Leslie storyline. The choice of Eleanor Roosevelt as a romantic roleplay character is perfect Leslie Knope — she is so politically passionate that her foreplay involves First Ladies. 'Eleanor likes the tongue' is a devastating line from Chris — he processed this audio long enough to form opinions about Eleanor Roosevelt's kissing style. The joke is completely specific to these characters and could not exist in any other show. Very high quotability and rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I've been working on this song all week. It's gonna blow your minds. It's called 'Tiny Dancer Times Tiny Dancer.'

jokes.text: Chris continues describing the butt-dial audio: 'Hey, show me Pelosi again.' Ben: 'Okay, lay down.' Then Leslie asks: 'Please tell me you hung up before Ruth Bader Ginsburg.' Chris: 'Unfortunately not.'
jokes.setup: The butt-dial revealed Eleanor Roosevelt roleplay; Leslie hopes it ended there
jokes.punchline: It did not — the roleplay extended through multiple political figures, with Ruth Bader Ginsburg as the apparent grand finale. 'Lay down' for Pelosi implies a different choreography than Eleanor. 'Unfortunately not' from Chris indicates RBG was particularly eventful.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from Eleanor Roosevelt to Nancy Pelosi to Ruth Bader Ginsburg is superbly constructed. Each political figure adds specificity and absurdity. 'Lay down' for Pelosi implies the roleplay has its own choreography per character. 'Unfortunately not' is the perfect understatement from Chris — he didn't want to know this about RBG but now he does. The escalating cringe and escalating commitment to the bit makes this slightly better than the initial reveal. The 'unfortunately not' button is perfectly delivered deadpan.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: She was a bright light in a dark tunnel. A shining beacon of hope that soared like a majestic eagle... riding on the back of a dolphin.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: And when life got her down, she would just take a running leap and fly away like a horse.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Please tell me you hung up before Ruth Bader Ginsburg.' Ron: 'Unfortunately not.'
jokes.setup: The presidential role-play escalation has been building; Leslie fears the worst.
jokes.punchline: 'Unfortunately not.' — Ruth Bader Ginsburg is the final, most absurd escalation, and Ron has witnessed it all.
jokes.explanation: The peak of the episode's best comedic sequence. RBG as the comedic terminus of the presidential role-play is both unexpected and perfect — she's the most unlikely choice, which makes her the funniest. 'Unfortunately not' is two words that do maximum damage. Nearly perfect economy and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't like it. Torches are for people who don't have the confidence to use a regular light switch.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, it's just for the opening ceremony.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: A torch is a symbol of weakness. I need to carry something that represents strength and independence. Like a flashlight. A very expensive flashlight.

jokes.text: Ron warns them they'll get fired. Ben explains: 'Oh, President Reagan, my blazer popped open. Well, Maggie Thatcher, let me help you with that. It's gonna be a bumpy ride to this summit meeting. Our countries have had a very... special relationship...'
jokes.setup: Ron is trying to explain the seriousness of getting caught; Ben seems to be recounting more roleplay examples to demonstrate they're being 'careful'
jokes.punchline: Ben demonstrates their 'care' by narrating more presidential roleplay — this time Reagan and Thatcher — which proves the exact opposite of discretion
jokes.explanation: The Reagan/Thatcher roleplay is the third escalation of this running gag and adds a trans-Atlantic dimension (American/British leader pairing) that deepens the joke. 'A bumpy ride to this summit meeting' and 'our countries have had a very special relationship' are excellent because they're simultaneously diplomatic rhetoric AND double entendres. Ron's horrified expression watching this demonstration is implied and hilarious. The writing here is sharp — these are actual things Reagan and Thatcher said/discussed, repurposed as foreplay.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I cried once. When I was 7 and my horse died. I cried so hard that I was dehydrated for three days after that. Dated a woman for two years once. Sometime our love was passionate, sometimes it was affectionate. It was wonderful.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: She left me. I was not moved. And I cried when my horse died.

jokes.text: Andy's work-in-progress memorial song for Li'l Sebastian: 'In my heart, I'm sad you had to die. Li'l horse, spread your wings and learn to fly.' — Ron: 'Horses don't fly.' Andy: 'That's why I'm telling him, learn to fly.'
jokes.setup: Ron points out the zoological error: horses don't fly
jokes.punchline: Andy defends the lyric as instructional — he's teaching the horse to fly, not describing a known capability
jokes.explanation: Andy's logic is airtight within its own framework — he's not describing horse flight as a fact, he's encouraging the horse to discover it. Ron's deadpan literal objection vs. Andy's earnest literal defense creates a perfect comedic collision. The joke works because both characters are being completely sincere. Andy's childlike logic about teaching dead horses aeronautics is very on-brand.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I substituted the nitrogen in the fertilizer with helium to make it lighter.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry, that's not how chemistry works!

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Well, it seemed like a good idea at the time.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We need to evacuate immediately!

jokes.text: Andy's current draft lyrics: 'You're a champion little horse / And you're dead / You're the champion of death'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks to hear the best version of the song so far
jokes.punchline: Andy's draft pivots immediately from celebration to declaration of death and then crowns the horse 'champion of death' — a metal achievement rather than an honor
jokes.explanation: The brevity here is the joke — three lines, and Andy has already declared the horse a death champion. The arc from 'champion little horse' to 'champion of death' in nine words is both absurd and somehow Andy's sincere best effort. The directness of 'And you're dead' as a lyric is brilliantly blunt. This is completely Andy Dwyer and works because he's genuinely trying.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I can't tell if Ron's angry or sad. His eyebrows are gone.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm both, Jerry.

jokes.text: Leslie suggests Andy try to write 'without the word dead so much. Or death or you're dead.' — implying he's used all three variants in what we heard
jokes.setup: Andy has played his draft; Leslie needs to give constructive feedback
jokes.punchline: Leslie has to specifically exclude three nearly-identical variants of 'dead' as acceptable lyric words, revealing Andy has already used all of them
jokes.explanation: The callback and enumeration ('dead... or death... or you're dead') implies Andy used all available forms of the concept in one short song. Leslie's patient specificity in her feedback is a nice character note — she's being a thoughtful producer while still being horrified by the material.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tom is selfish, arrogant, and a terrible friend. He's also stupid, lazy, and has no real skills or talents whatsoever. He's a burden on this office and a burden on society.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: But... I need him. I don't know why, but I do. Please don't ever leave.

jokes.text: Ben and Leslie discuss their 'professional hug' protocol: Ben demonstrates a stilted 'Oh, congratulations' hug as what would look professional
jokes.setup: They're establishing rules for behavior at work to avoid detection
jokes.punchline: Ben's 'professional hug' is obviously just a regular affectionate hug rebranded, and they're both fooling themselves about its invisibility
jokes.explanation: A solid situational comedy beat — the contrast between their attempt at professionalism and the obvious transparency of the 'professional hug' is the joke. Physical comedy that reads through dialogue. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy II
dialogue.line: Ron! I heard about your little memorial service. How touching.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Tammy.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy II
dialogue.line: And Glenn! My two favorite men in one place. You both came to mourn me?

dialogue.speaker: Glenn Dusnick
dialogue.line: We're not—

dialogue.speaker: Tammy II
dialogue.line: Don't be modest. We all know we were lovers. Both of you. At the same time. It's fine, I'm not mad.

jokes.text: The maintenance worker they were trying to keep secret walks in mid-hug and says 'Hey, lovebirds. What do I do with this?'
jokes.setup: Ben and Leslie have just convincingly argued they can get away with the 'professional hug'
jokes.punchline: Immediate contradiction: caught again, by another person, mid-demonstration of the professional hug
jokes.explanation: The structural irony is perfect: they just demonstrated the hug as safe and immediately get caught doing it. 'Hey, lovebirds' is a casual greeting that obliterates their whole scheme. The joke is earned by the setup, even if the beat itself is a familiar 'caught in the act' structure.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I would rather have severe burns on my face than spend one more second with Tammy.

jokes.text: Leslie tallies: 'So my mom, Ron, Ann, and that guy.' — updating the list of people who know about her relationship
jokes.setup: Leslie has been managing the list of people who know about her and Ben
jokes.punchline: The list has just grown by a random maintenance worker, and Leslie's matter-of-fact inventory of 'and that guy' is the comedic acknowledgment
jokes.explanation: Part of the running gag of the secret relationship's progressive exposure. 'That guy' is the right word choice — she doesn't even know his name, making his addition to the list both funny and faintly ominous. The list-keeping is very Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Chris, you have to stop exercising so much. Your tendonitis is getting worse.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Ann, I only do a thousand push-ups every morning, a five-mile run before work, fifty pull-ups on my lunch break, and then I do CrossFit for three hours after work.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's insane!

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Plus on weekends I do Insanity workout videos and then I climb a mountain just for fun.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Chris, that's not normal exercise. That's a cry for help.

jokes.text: Tom presents ribbons for the memorial — 'Which one floats your penis?' — all of which appear identical black ribbons. Jerry points this out. Tom lectures about the subtle distinctions: 'Obsidian, onyx, midnight, lost soul, rolling blackout, sleeping panther, and void by Armani.'
jokes.setup: Tom wants Jerry to choose between memorial ribbons
jokes.punchline: Tom has names for seven imperceptibly different shades of black, each more pretentious than the last, culminating in 'void by Armani'
jokes.explanation: The list of black ribbon names is one of the episode's highlights. The escalation of pretension — 'obsidian' (geological) to 'onyx' (gemstone) to 'midnight' (poetic) to 'lost soul' (emo) to 'rolling blackout' (political) to 'sleeping panther' (???) to 'void by Armani' (designer existential crisis) — is expertly crafted. Each name is funnier than the last. 'Void by Armani' is the perfect final destination. This is very specifically Tom Haverford and could not be attributed to any other character. Also: 'Which one floats your penis?' as an opener is a great throwaway.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I've planned a romantic evening for us. I've calculated the optimal route through the park for a moonlit walk that maximizes calorie burn while minimizing joint impact.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Chris, that's not romantic.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I've also prepared a low-sodium, high-protein dinner with a precise macronutrient ratio. And I color-coded the evening's schedule for maximum efficiency.

jokes.text: Tom holds up one of the ribbons and asks Jerry: 'Hey, Jerry, does this look black to you, too?' — implying he is asking if Jerry can even perceive the difference
jokes.setup: Jerry said all the ribbons look black to him
jokes.punchline: Tom sarcastically validates Jerry's inability to perceive the distinctions by asking if 'this one' also looks black — implying Jerry's aesthetic sense is deficient
jokes.explanation: A decent button on the previous ribbon joke, but less sharp than the setup. Tom condescending to Jerry's taste is an established dynamic that works here without adding much new. Functional coda.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: You charged me $12 for a $5 item.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Well, you have a weird face.

jokes.text: Chris calls Ann to ask if tendonitis is 'symptomatic of something larger' — after an elaborate buildup implying a serious question
jokes.setup: Chris creates a formal, portentous setup — 'I need to ask you a question, and if you're uncomfortable answering it...' — suggesting something deeply personal
jokes.punchline: The serious question is medical hypochondria: is tendonitis a sign of something worse?
jokes.explanation: The formal setup suggests Chris is about to ask Ann something emotionally significant about their relationship; the medical deflation is a good misdirection. His hypochondria and self-absorption come through. The joke also works on an emotional level: Chris uses medical concern as a way to approach Ann while avoiding the actual emotional conversation.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Where are you going, Glenn? To pound town?

dialogue.speaker: Glenn
dialogue.line: No, I'm taking the express train to deep tunnel station, population: me.

jokes.text: Ann to Chris: 'I'm not your nurse, and I'm not your girlfriend — I thought I was twice, and I was wrong, which was embarrassing.'
jokes.setup: Ann pushes back on Chris using her for medical advice
jokes.punchline: 'I thought I was [your girlfriend] twice, and I was wrong, which was embarrassing' — Ann summarizes the entire failed relationship history with dry self-deprecating honesty
jokes.explanation: Ann's 'which was embarrassing' is the key word — it's honest and funny and a little sad, which is the right emotional register for this storyline. The 'twice' specification shows she's been keeping count. Strong character moment that gets a laugh while doing real character work. Economy is good.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: I hired Tessa because she's got real business acumen, you know? She understands the entrepreneurial spirit.

dialogue.speaker: Tessa
dialogue.line: Do I get a company car?

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: We haven't even started yet.

dialogue.speaker: Tessa
dialogue.line: A Range Rover?

jokes.text: Chris says: 'I do hope we can be friends before I die.' — intending it as a gracious olive branch but accidentally making it about his imminent mortality
jokes.setup: Chris accepts Ann's rejection gracefully and expresses hope for friendship
jokes.punchline: The qualifier 'before I die' — which a healthy person would not add to this sentence — reveals Chris is still processing his tendonitis as a terminal diagnosis
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — five words ('before I die') do all the comedic work. The callback to Chris's overreaction to tendonitis is seamlessly integrated into an otherwise sincere moment. The contrast between Chris's genuine emotional generosity and his catastrophizing is very true to the character.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Why is the petty cash in the toilet bowl?

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Because it's a liquid asset.

jokes.text: Ben claims Leslie hugged him because she 'won the MacArthur Genius Grant.' He and Leslie then both say 'Yeah' in unconvincing unison.
jokes.setup: They need to explain away the hug to Chris
jokes.punchline: Ben invents the MacArthur Genius Grant as the cover story; both he and Leslie affirm it with exactly zero conviction
jokes.explanation: The MacArthur Genius Grant is a nice choice of lie — both prestigious enough to warrant a hug and specific enough to sound credible if you don't examine it. The synchronous 'Yeah' from both of them would play brilliantly as an obviously rehearsed, awkward affirmation. Their bad lying is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: You gotta strike while the iron is hot and plant your seeds in fertile ground, you know what I'm saying? That's how you build a client base.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: First you gotta get your foot in the door, then you climb the ladder, then you're gonna be rolling in it like a dog in mud.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: It's all about the long game mixed with the short con, bro. You just gotta believe in yourself and also commit light fraud.

jokes.text: Ben tells Chris to 'take the rest of the day off... get a massage.' Leslie adds: 'I have a gift certificate, actually. My mom gave it to me for you.'
jokes.setup: They're trying to get Chris to leave so he stops noticing their relationship
jokes.punchline: Leslie casually claims to have a gift certificate from her mom specifically given to her for Chris — an impossibly convenient and specific piece of bribery that makes no chronological sense
jokes.explanation: The absurdity of Leslie's mom pre-emptively giving her a gift certificate for Chris's future massage is funny because it implies a weird level of maternal foresight. Chris's enthusiasm ('Oh, my God. Yes!') at believing this completely is also funny — he's so susceptible to positive gestures. Solid character-specific joke.

jokes.text: Ben calls Chris 'George' when saying goodbye, having forgotten Chris's name in the moment — Leslie says 'Yes' and both thank 'George'
jokes.setup: Ben and Leslie are wrapping up their fake-natural goodbye to Chris
jokes.punchline: Ben calls Chris 'George' — clearly a brain malfunction under stress — and Leslie goes along with it rather than correcting it
jokes.explanation: The wrong-name panic is a classic cringe beat, elevated here by Leslie immediately committing to the error rather than correcting it. The implication that Chris just accepts being called George (or doesn't notice, because Chris is that gracious) adds to the absurdity.

jokes.text: 'Not only was Coconut a friend, but she was also a lover. Our deepest sympathy is with you.' Then: 'Coconut just took a dump on the stage. We gotta clean that up. Code red. Coconut just took a dump onstage.'
jokes.setup: The ceremony introduces Coconut as Li'l Sebastian's friend and 'also a lover'
jokes.punchline: Coconut immediately defecates on the stage, triggering a 'code red' that collapses the ceremony's dignity
jokes.explanation: The setup of Coconut as a 'lover' makes the defecation particularly undignified — this is Sebastian's girlfriend pooping on his memorial. The transition from 'deepest sympathy' to 'code red' is a sharp tonal collapse. Jean-Ralphio repeating the code red announcement twice ('Code red. Coconut just took a dump onstage') as if the mic is still hot is an extra layer of comedy.

jokes.text: Jerry refuses to get propane: 'No, what about my poem?' Leslie: 'No one wants you to read a poem, okay, Jerry? What everyone wants — what Li'l Sebastian wants — is for you to get propane.' Jerry: 'Fine. I'll do it for Li'l Sebastian.'
jokes.setup: Leslie needs Jerry for an errand; Jerry was supposed to read a poem
jokes.punchline: Leslie's devastating 'No one wants you to read a poem' redirects through Li'l Sebastian as a moral authority — and Jerry is moved by this
jokes.explanation: Multiple layers: Jerry's excitement about his Dante poem is immediately extinguished ('No one wants you to read a poem, okay, Jerry?'), which is a characteristically brutal Jerry dismissal. Leslie then invokes Li'l Sebastian as a higher moral authority who also wants propane, which is both absurd and effective. Jerry's capitulation via 'I'll do it for Li'l Sebastian' is the character surrendering to the horse's posthumous authority. Excellent economy.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio's intro to the Entertainment 7Twenty video presentation: 'Hope you brought a change of clothes. 'Cause your eyes are about to piss tears. You nasty.'
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio is about to introduce a memorial video
jokes.punchline: 'Your eyes are about to piss tears. You nasty.' — an entirely inappropriate way to introduce a funeral tribute that somehow also functions as a compliment
jokes.explanation: 'Your eyes are about to piss tears' is a genuinely excellent phrase — vulgar enough to be startling at a memorial, vivid enough to be memorable, and delivered with pride. 'You nasty' as a closer is strange and perfect — it turns the anticipated emotional impact into something the audience should be ashamed of wanting. This is completely Jean-Ralphio and could only happen at an Entertainment 7Twenty-produced memorial. High quotability. One of the episode's most memorable lines.

jokes.text: The memorial video montage poses deep philosophical questions — 'Who are we? Where are we going in life? What is the meaning of all of this?' — and answers: 'These are questions Li'l Sebastian never had to answer because he was a horse.'
jokes.setup: The video builds to what seems like a profound meditation on mortality and meaning
jokes.punchline: The existential questions are resolved by pointing out that Sebastian, as a horse, simply didn't have to deal with them — and that's the real lesson
jokes.explanation: The rhetorical structure here is genuinely clever: the video sets up profound existential questions and delivers a non-answer that is simultaneously deflating and oddly comforting. 'He was a horse' as the philosophical resolution is a great joke because it's technically true and completely useless. The joke has something real to say about why we love simple creatures — they don't suffer the anxieties we do. That added depth gives it rewatch value.

jokes.text: Tom pitching the company to Jean-Ralphio while the memorial video plays: 'I'm the bank. You're the money.' Jean-Ralphio: 'I'm Thelma, you're Louise. You can't die full of regret.' Tom: 'Why don't you live your life like that cow from the video?' Jean-Ralphio: 'He was a horse.'
jokes.setup: Tom and Jean-Ralphio are having a business conversation in the middle of the memorial service
jokes.punchline: Tom calls Li'l Sebastian 'that cow from the video' — getting the basic species wrong of the horse the whole ceremony is about — and Jean-Ralphio corrects him
jokes.explanation: Tom calling Sebastian a cow is the punchline — it reveals how little either of them actually cares about the horse they're exploiting for publicity. The irony of Jean-Ralphio (who also doesn't care) being the one to correct the species is a nice double-irony. 'I'm Thelma, you're Louise' as a business partnership metaphor is also good — it implies they'll drive off a cliff, which is thematically accurate for their business prospects.

jokes.text: Andy announces his song: 'What's 5,000 times better than a candle in the wind? This song is called 5,000 Candles in the Wind.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asked Andy for something '5,000 times better than Candle in the Wind' (joke 16 area)
jokes.punchline: Andy takes the instruction literally and titles the song '5,000 Candles in the Wind' — quantifying the improvement rather than qualitatively exceeding it
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes and genuinely excellent comedy writing. Andy's literal interpretation of the '5,000 times better' instruction as a song title is both stupid and somehow perfect — he's not wrong that having 5,000 candles in the wind is quantitatively superior to one. The announcement of the title with a rhetorical question is a superb structure. The callback payoff is earned and the title itself is instantly iconic within the show's universe. '5,000 Candles in the Wind' became a real cultural touchstone for Parks fans. Very high quotability.

jokes.text: Andy performs '5,000 Candles in the Wind' — a genuinely heartfelt song about Li'l Sebastian going to heaven, trading legs for angel wings and taking 'a running leap' to fly
jokes.setup: The song has been set up as Andy's work-in-progress which previously included 'champion of death'
jokes.punchline: The song is... actually really good? Sweet, sincere, and musically competent — the joke is that Andy Dwyer, who sleeps on a futon and was paid $50, produced something genuinely moving
jokes.explanation: The comedy of '5,000 Candles in the Wind' as performed is the subversion of every setup: Andy was paid $50, had a draft that said 'champion of death,' sleeps on a futon — and delivers something genuinely lovely. The callback to 'take a running leap and learn to fly' references Ron's earlier 'horses don't fly' objection. The joke is sustained by the audience caring about both Sebastian and Andy, making the sincerity of the performance land as comedy-through-earned-emotion. This is the episode's emotional center and it works comedically because of how wrong all the setups suggested it would go.

jokes.text: Leslie discovers the ceremony assignments have completely cascaded: Perd Hapley is unveiling the memorial stone because Joe from sewage had to hand out armbands, and Perd had to fill in for Mortenson, and Mortenson had to fill in for Howser. And Donna is reading Jerry's Italian poem.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks why Perd Hapley is doing the memorial stone unveiling
jokes.punchline: A complete chain of cascading substitutions has shuffled every single job, ending with Donna reading a 13th-century Italian poem
jokes.explanation: The Rube Goldberg chain of incompetent substitutions is a good bureaucratic chaos joke — very Parks and Rec. The image of Donna unexpectedly performing Dante is the best element. The joke rewards the specificity of each substitution link in the chain. Solid structural setup for the subsequent 'this is a mess' beat.

jokes.text: Ron furiously confronts Leslie: 'What the hell, Leslie? I thought I was supposed to lay the ceremonial wreath. Why is Councilman Howser doing it?' Leslie: 'Because you are doing something better. You are lighting the memorial flame, which is the greatest honor of all.' Ron: 'Oh, my God. Ron, congratulations. I saved it for you, Ron.'
jokes.setup: Ron is angry about being moved from wreath-laying; Leslie needs him to light the flame instead
jokes.punchline: Leslie's flattery is so naked and effective that Ron immediately gives himself the congratulation she prompted him toward — congratulating himself in the third person
jokes.explanation: Ron Swanson congratulating himself in the third person ('Oh, my God. Ron, congratulations.') after being played by Leslie is superb character comedy. The joke works because Ron is simultaneously un-manipulable (on matters of principle) and completely susceptible (to genuine honor). Leslie's salesmanship is matched perfectly by Ron's instant capitulation. The self-directed 'congratulations' shows Ron has already internalized the honor as real. Great character integration.

jokes.text: Ron: 'I think if you would know one thing about me, it would be that I prefer laying wreaths to lighting torches.'
jokes.setup: Leslie sold Ron on the torch-lighting as 'the greatest honor'; Ron now clarifies his actual preference
jokes.punchline: Ron has a clear, considered preference between these two highly specific ceremonial activities — wreath-laying over torch-lighting — stated as if it's defining biographical information
jokes.explanation: This is Ron Swanson at his most perfectly himself. The joke is that this IS defining biographical information for Ron — he has thought about this, he has a position on it, and he will state it with the gravity of a constitutional amendment. 'I think if you would know one thing about me' makes it sound like a will reading. The specificity of the preference is what makes it land — not 'I prefer X to Y generally' but this exact ceremonial distinction. Economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: Ron talking-head: 'I have cried twice in my life. Once when I was seven, and I was hit by a school bus. And then again when I heard that Li'l Sebastian had passed.'
jokes.setup: Ron is explaining his emotional state regarding Li'l Sebastian's death
jokes.punchline: Ron's only two lifetime cries are (1) being physically struck by a school bus and (2) Li'l Sebastian's death — placing a horse's passing on equal emotional footing with a childhood vehicular trauma
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke and one of the best Ron Swanson lines in the entire series. The structure is flawless: the setup of 'I have cried twice in my life' immediately signals something extraordinary; the first instance (being hit by a school bus at seven) is appropriately traumatic and darkly specific; the second instance — a mini-horse dying — is the punchline, because it places Sebastian on equal emotional footing with childhood vehicular trauma. The joke is entirely impossible without Ron's specific character and his established love for Li'l Sebastian. Every word is necessary. 'Twice' rather than 'a few times' creates a perfect sense of constraint. The structure is as close to perfect as sitcom writing gets. Comparable to the 9.5 anchor example in quality.

jokes.text: Jerry puts lighter fluid instead of propane in the eternal flame, causing a massive fireball that burns off Ron's eyebrows. Tom and Leslie, terrified, immediately say: 'We planned that! Wow, wow!' / 'We planned that. Yay!'
jokes.setup: Ron was lighting the eternal flame; Jerry was supposed to get propane but got lighter fluid instead
jokes.punchline: A fireball engulfs the stage area; Tom and Leslie — wanting the ceremony to seem intentional — instantly claim it was planned
jokes.explanation: The payoff to Jerry's propane errand is excellent — the logical escalation of Jerry incompetence (propane → lighter fluid → fireball) is perfectly calibrated. Tom and Leslie's instant PR spin ('We planned that!') is pitch-perfect emergency crisis management. The physical comedy of Ron losing his eyebrows sets up joke 67. The crowd cheering 'Yay!' suggests the fireball WAS well-received, which makes the cover story accidentally true.

jokes.text: After the fireball, Leslie yells 'We planned that! Wow, wow!' as cover. Then again: 'We planned that.'
jokes.setup: A fireball has accidentally erupted at the memorial.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's crowd-management instinct kicks in: she claims it was intentional, repeating 'We planned that' with decreasing conviction.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's reflex to claim incompetence as planning is deeply in character — her ability to spin anything as intentional is a defining trait. The repetition of 'We planned that' with diminishing certainty is the key beat. Highly quotable in context.

jokes.text: Leslie apologizes to Ron: 'I guess I put too much fuel in the torch.' Ron: 'Oh, I don't know, Jerry. I think you're being hard on yourself.' Leslie: 'Ron, are you mad at me? 'Cause without eyebrows, I can't really tell.'
jokes.setup: Ron's eyebrows have been burned off; Leslie is trying to read his emotional state
jokes.punchline: 'Without eyebrows, I can't really tell' — eyebrows being fundamental to reading facial expressions; Ron's burned-off eyebrows make his emotional state genuinely unreadable
jokes.explanation: 'Without eyebrows, I can't really tell' is one of the episode's best lines. It's both literally true (eyebrows are critical to facial expression reading) and perfectly chosen to describe Ron Swanson specifically — a man whose eyebrows do enormous expressive work given his otherwise stony face. The joke is economical and character-specific. The fact that the line works as both sincere concern AND a great punchline makes it exceptional. Also note: Ron mixes up Leslie and Jerry in his response ('I don't know, Jerry' when talking to Leslie) suggesting the fireball did indeed affect him — a subtle additional layer.

jokes.text: Ron's talking-head: 'Ron Swanson loves his facial hair. And we burned it off.' — referring to himself in the third person with devastated finality
jokes.setup: Ron is processing the loss of his eyebrows and mustache in the fireball
jokes.punchline: Ron refers to himself in the third person as 'Ron Swanson' while delivering the tragedy of his facial hair loss with the gravity of a national disaster
jokes.explanation: Devastatingly good Ron Swanson character comedy. The third-person construction — 'Ron Swanson loves his facial hair' — is both grandiose and immediately crushed by '...and we burned it off.' The simplicity of the second sentence against the stately formality of the first is the perfect comedic structure. The 'we' is also interesting — Ron acknowledges complicity in the group disaster. This is Ron Swanson's mustache receiving an obituary, which is funny on its own terms. Very high character integration and economy.

jokes.text: Ron to Tom: 'You have no interest in government work, and you slow everything down with your selfish attitude. I'd love for you to stick around, Tommy. It'll be damn hard to replace you.'
jokes.setup: Ron is advising Tom on whether to leave his government job for Jean-Ralphio's company
jokes.punchline: Ron gives a brutally honest negative performance review — no interest, selfish, slows things down — and THEN says he'd love for Tom to stay and it'll be 'damn hard to replace you'
jokes.explanation: This is Ron's love language perfectly articulated. The structure — brutal honest insult followed immediately by sincere sentiment — is a Ron Swanson signature and it lands with maximum emotional impact because we believe both things. He genuinely thinks Tom slows everything down AND genuinely doesn't want him to leave. The juxtaposition makes the 'damn hard to replace you' land as both funny and touching. The joke is entirely specific to Ron's character and his particular relationship with Tom. One of the episode's emotionally strongest jokes.

jokes.text: Tammy One appears and says: 'Two of my lovers in one place. What a coincidence.'
jokes.setup: Ron and Tom are having a quiet emotional moment
jokes.punchline: Tammy One appears and claims both Ron and Tom as past lovers simultaneously — a dark, funny, and disturbing claim
jokes.explanation: Tammy One's entrance line is excellent — 'two of my lovers in one place' is genuinely alarming (especially re: Tom) and delivered with predatory cheer. The implication about Tom is new information that recontextualizes everything. Very good economy: one sentence does maximum character work for a new character. The 'What a coincidence' closer is the right deadpan button.

jokes.text: Tammy One about Ron's burned face: 'Ooh, what happened here? And more importantly, does the carpet match the face?'
jokes.setup: Tammy One notices Ron's eyebrow-less, burned face
jokes.punchline: She inverts the 'does the carpet match the drapes?' idiom, replacing 'drapes' with 'face' — asking if his body hair also got burned — a mean but clever wordplay
jokes.explanation: This is a very clever wordplay joke. 'Does the carpet match the face?' subverts the idiom perfectly — instead of asking about hair color consistency, it's asking whether Ron's burned, hairless face matches the rest of his body hair situation. The inversion is tight and the delivery is cold-blooded, which is perfect for Tammy One. High quotability and originality. One of the episode's best pure wordplay moments.

jokes.text: Ron to Tammy One: 'If you're looking for trouble, take it somewhere else. An hour ago, a giant fireball consumed my entire face. And it was far preferable to spending another second with you.'
jokes.setup: Tammy One is provocative and threatening; Ron responds
jokes.punchline: Ron states with complete sincerity that a literal fireball consuming his face was preferable to Tammy One — the most extreme possible comparison for how much he dislikes her
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest jokes. The structure is perfect: Ron establishes the horrific context (giant fireball, entire face consumed), then delivers the devastating comparative: that experience was better than Tammy One. The understatement of 'far preferable' in the context of face-consuming fireballs is extremely Ron Swanson. The callback to the fireball gives this maximum payoff. Highly quotable and a standout line in Ron's entire character arc.

jokes.text: Tammy One: 'Tell that to your pants-tent.' Ron: 'It's just the way I'm standing.'
jokes.setup: Ron has just declared Tammy One worse than a fireball to the face
jokes.punchline: Tammy One points out Ron's physical arousal despite his claimed contempt; Ron denies it with an anatomically implausible excuse
jokes.explanation: 'Tell that to your pants-tent' is an excellent line — it undercuts Ron's whole rejection monologue with physical evidence of the opposite. 'It's just the way I'm standing' is the perfect Ron Swanson response: maintain the position with absurd confidence despite incontrovertible evidence. The Tammy/Ron dynamic (she both repels and attracts him) is perfectly captured in two lines. Very high character integration and economy.

jokes.text: Chris and Ann bond over his tendonitis: Ann: 'You need to relax. You're in great shape. For a 44-year-old.' Chris: 'Yeah. That's how old you are, man.'
jokes.setup: Ann is reassuring Chris about his health
jokes.punchline: Ann slightly undercuts her reassurance with 'for a 44-year-old'; Chris needs a beat to process and then confirms it as a statement of fact about himself
jokes.explanation: The callback to Chris's sensitivity about his age works here — Ann accidentally deploys the same qualifier as the mean doctor, but Chris has processed it enough to accept it with equanimity. 'That's how old you are, man' is a nice gently defeated response. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Chris: 'I don't like thinking about death. Death is the opposite of...' Ann: 'Being alive?' Chris: 'Exactly.'
jokes.setup: Chris trails off while searching for the opposite of death
jokes.punchline: Ann offers 'being alive' as the obvious completion; Chris accepts this as an insightful observation
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Chris — a man of infinite positivity and deep philosophical engagement — gets stumped looking for the opposite of death and needs Ann to supply 'being alive.' His sincere 'Exactly' suggests this was actually illuminating for him. The gap between Chris's self-image as a deep thinker and his need for this most basic answer is the joke. Economy is strong.

jokes.text: Chris and Ann declare themselves friends: 'What the hell. Friends.' / 'Ann Perkins.' / 'Chris Traeger.' Chris then says: 'What's the point in doing 10,000 push-ups if you're gonna do them alone? I'd much rather do 5,000 push-ups with a wonderful woman. Sitting on my back to increase my resistance.'
jokes.setup: Chris and Ann have reconciled into friendship; Chris reflects on his exercise philosophy
jokes.punchline: What sounds like a metaphor for companionship ('why do push-ups alone') is revealed to be a literal proposition — having Ann sit on his back during push-ups — stated as a romantic offer
jokes.explanation: The setup sounds like a metaphorical statement about loneliness and companionship; the reveal that it's literally about weighted push-ups — and that Chris thinks this is a romantic offer — is a good misdirection payoff. Very Chris: he can turn exercise into an intimate suggestion. The 'sitting on my back to increase my resistance' is the perfect specific detail that makes the literal reading land.

jokes.text: Andy sells CDs after the memorial: '18 bucks each, $40 for the set.' Audience member: 'That doesn't add up.' Andy: 'You don't add up.'
jokes.setup: Andy is pricing his merch and someone points out the math doesn't work
jokes.punchline: 'You don't add up' — a retort that makes no sense as a comeback but is delivered with total confidence
jokes.explanation: Five words, perfect Andy Dwyer. 'You don't add up' is a non-sequitur comeback to a math complaint that somehow works as a dismissal — it sounds like a devastating response even though it means nothing. The economy is near-perfect. Very Andy: complete confidence in the face of being demonstrably wrong. This is a joke that gets better the more you think about it, which is rare for a five-word line.

jokes.text: Andy proposes to April: 'April, I need to ask you something, and it's the biggest thing I've ever asked anybody in my entire life.' April: 'Honey, we're already married.' Andy: 'No, this is way more important than that.' Asks her to be his manager.
jokes.setup: Andy builds up to 'the biggest thing I've ever asked anybody in my entire life' — the setup suggests something of profound personal significance
jokes.punchline: He asks her to be his music manager — something he clearly values more than their marriage, which he casually dismisses as 'way more important than that'
jokes.explanation: Textbook misdirection structure executed perfectly.
